title: Staged hypershard session serialization - scratchpad
content:
Goal / motivation:
- Build a lightweight, progressive serialization format and runtime flow to offload active LLM sessions across multiple storage tiers (RAM -> NVMe -> S3-like cold store) with minimal tail-latency impact and bounded extra cost.
- Support fast local rehydrate for hot sessions and progressive reassembly for long-context replays.
- Allow operator policy (cost vs latency vs reliability) to control staging/eviction.

Background and constraints (notes):
- Current KV-cache snapshot offload is monolithic: snapshot whole session or nothing. This leads to big cold-starts when rehydrating long contexts.
- Hypersharding: split session state into many small shard blobs (by token-range, chunked KV, or embedding groups). Small pieces enable partial rehydration and parallel fetch.
- Must interop with existing prefix-caching and attention-kv layouts.
- Security: still must obey tenant isolation and CC encryption; metadata must not leak prompt content.

Design sketch (high-level):
1) Session manifest (tiny, always-resident):
   - session_id, version, owner_tenant, sequence of shards with locators + bloom/summary, current head pointer, compression+crypto metadata, last_active_ts.
   - manifest stays in fast cache (memtable).
2) Shard layout: micro-blobs (4–64KB target) each containing:
   - shard_id (session, index), shard_type (kv, tokens, tooling), minimal summary (min/max token index), small checksum, TTL-tier target.
   - optional inlined small embeddings or pointer to embedding-bundle object.
3) Eviction policy: staged tiers with graceful eviction:
   - Tier0: in-memory. Tier1: local NVMe (fast rehydrate). Tier2: regional object store. Tier3: archival (cold).
   - Policy dsl: keep X recent shards in Tier0, keep hot shards pinned; heuristics using access frequency + recency + user-specified importance labels.

API shapes (draft):
- GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/manifest -> returns manifest with shard index + health flags
- POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/shards/fetch (body: [shard_ids], fetch_mode=fast|blocking|prefetch) -> stream shards as NDJSON, fields: shard_id, payload_b64, meta
- POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/shards/pin -> pin shards to Tier0 / TTL override
- PUT /v1/sessions/{sid}/shards -> upload new shard (used by offload flow)

Example manifest (pseudo):
{
  "session_id": "s-123",
  "version": "v0.1",
  "shard_index": [
    {"id":"s-123-0001","type":"kv","range":[0,127],"tier":"tier0","crc":"..."},
    {"id":"s-123-0002","type":"tokens","range":[128,511],"tier":"tier1","crc":"..."}
  ],
  "head": 512,
  "last_active": "2026-02-19T21:10:00Z"
}

Progressive rehydrate flow (happy path):
- Ingress receives request referencing session S and context pointers. Runtime consults manifest -> finds missing shards.
- Issue prefetch request with fetch_mode=fast for shards that are adjacent to the head; start streaming them to worker while continuing generation with available context.
- If model asks for older context not present, runtime issues blocking fetch for specific shard(s) and stalls generation minimal time (bounded by SLO).
- For large-range retrievals, parallel fetch across Tier1 + Tier2 with backoff; merge shards on arrival.

Heuristics we should prototype: (experiments)
- Shard sizing impact: experiment with 4KB, 16KB, 64KB (perf + cost)
- Bloom vs summary: store small bloom filter for quick membership test rather than fetching contents
- Rehydration window: prefetch N shards around head where N is dynamic from observed rehits
- Credit accounting: maintain per-session prefetch budget to avoid runaway egress cost

Data model tradeoffs / open questions:
- Inline vs pointer for embeddings: small embeddings inline speeds rehydrate but duplicates across shards increase storage cost.
- Checksum granularity vs repair cost: fine-grained checksums help corrupt detection but increase metadata size.
- Atomicity guarantees for manifest+shards on multi-writer traffic (concurrent session updates). Should we use optimistic CAS on manifest with epoch?

Operational telemetry (events to emit):
- shard_evicted {session_id, shard_id, from_tier, to_tier, reason}
- shard_fetch {session_id, shard_id, src_tier, latency_ms, bytes}
- manifest_mismatch {session_id, last_seen_version, current_version}
- rehydrate_block {session_id, missing_shards, stall_ms, call_id}
- prefetch_credit_deduct {session_id, amount, remaining}

SLO targets (draft):
- For hot head shards: rehydrate 95th <= 8ms (from Tier1 NVMe), 99th <= 30ms
- For typical blocking fetch from Tier2: 95th <= 120ms, 99th <= 500ms (depends on object store)
- Prefetch budget per session: default 64KB/sec (tunable)

Prototype checklist (MVP):
- [ ] Implement manifest in memtable + lightweight persistent index
- [ ] Offload job: chunk session -> shards -> upload to Tier1 and Tier2
- [ ] Fetch API to request by shard_id (batching + streaming)
- [ ] Basic prefetch policy: around-head prefetch N=3
- [ ] Telemetry for shard_fetch + evict
- [ ] Load test with synthetic long-context replay workload (mix cold/hot patterns)

Acceptance criteria for initial roll-in: (internal staging)
- Under a synthetic workload with 80% short-context hits and 20% long-context replays, average token latency increase <= 5% vs not-offloading baseline, and egress cost per session <= baseline * 1.8.
- No tenant can force unbounded egress via prefetch; observed credit enforcement works under stress.

Risks and mitigations:
- Hotspots: tiny shards may cause many parallel object calls. Mitigate by colocating Tier1 with NVMe sharding and request coalescing.
- Consistency during concurrent updates: use manifest CAS and per-shard write-locks for writer-side choreography.
- Cost blowouts from aggressive prefetch: implement exponential backoff + budget enforcement + operator throttle.

Prototype notes / implementation hints:
- Keep shard identifiers simple and monotonic: {session}-{epoch}-{shard-idx}
- Use LZ4 or Zstd framing per shard with small block sizes to favor partial reads.
- Store compact summary bloom in manifest (<= 128 bytes per shard) for quick membership test.
- For assembly, stream-by-merge (ordered by range) rather than building full in-memory buffer for huge sessions. Use async iterators.

Unresolved items / TODOs (brain dump):
- model-internal KV layout assumptions for fastest merge (need to sync with attention-kv team)
- UX for pinning shards from Console (pin/unpin UI + quota implications)
- Cold-store lifecycle: TTL ladder and archival deletion policy tied to customer contract
- Security review: ensure shards are encrypted at rest + keys rotate safe for partial-shard reads

Notes to self / quick experiments to try next week:
- run benchmark with 20k sessions, each with 1.2MB context, compare 16KB vs 64KB shards on latency tail
- implement a small in-memory bloom filter prototype to test false-positive rate vs size

Slack threads / references:
- Slack: #eng-serving-runtime thread "session-hypersharding" (recent discussion)
- Confluence draft: CONF-SESSION-REHY-42 (linked above)
- Jira spike: JIRA-OPS-6789 (experiment tracking)

If this grows beyond a scratchpad: move to a spec doc with sequence diagrams and clear API contract + JSON Schema for manifest/shard objects.

-- Ava
